name: 1-Androsterone (1-Andro)

lead: 1-Androsterone is an oral designer steroid sold as a supplement for muscle gain. It is a chemical variant of DHEA.
It appears in the literature mainly because a seized product was analysed so labs could detect it in urine. No human trials of its effects were found.

paras: It is described as a prohormone that converts to 1-testosterone and related androgens, which act on the androgen receptor.
No safety data from human trials exist. Authorities and anti-doping agencies consider such designer androgens related to anabolic steroids.

lead: 1-Androsterone, also sold as 1-Andro or 1-DHEA, is a synthetic oral androgen sold online as a "dietary supplement" for muscle gain. Chemically it is 3β-hydroxy-5α-androst-1-en-17-one, a positional isomer of the hormone DHEA.[1][2]

It is described as a prohormone that is converted in the body to 1-testosterone (dihydroboldenone) and related compounds.[1] The compound is documented mainly in analytical chemistry: a 2011 study identified it in a product seized by German criminal investigators and characterised its urinary elimination so it could be detected in doping control.[2]
No human efficacy or safety trials were found. Authorities and anti-doping bodies treat such designer androgens as pharmacologically related to anabolic steroids.[2]

paras: Wikipedia describes 1-androsterone as a prohormone that converts to 1-testosterone, 1-androstenedione and other 1-dehydrogenated androstanes, and lists it among androgen receptor agonists.[1] The sources reviewed give no pharmacokinetic data beyond urinary elimination work.[2]

The authors of the 2011 identification study note that new androgen analogues that were never approved as drugs are marketed as supplements, mainly advertised for muscle mass, and that government authorities and the World Anti-Doping Agency regard them as pharmacologically or chemically related to anabolic steroids.[2] Analytical chemists have also published methods for quantifying emerging designer steroids in supplements where reference materials are scarce.[3]
No studies found. The published literature consists of analytical studies on identification and urinary detection.[2][3]

timeline.event: A seized product sold as "1-Androsterone" is identified chemically and its urinary elimination described.[2]
